title: Jump Game II
description: Brute force to optimized: dynamic programming over every reachable pair versus greedy level by level boundary expansion.

blocks.text: Problem Summary: Given an array nums where nums[i] represents the maximum number of steps that can be jumped forward from index i, return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the last index. It is guaranteed the last index is always reachable.

blocks.text: Given an array nums where nums[i] represents the maximum number of steps that can be jumped forward from index i, return the minimum number of jumps needed to reach the last index. It is guaranteed the last index is always reachable.

blocks.title: Analogy: Stepping Stones Across a River
blocks.text: Like crossing a river on stepping stones where each stone shows how far forward it can launch a jump. The goal is not just to reach the far bank, but to do it using as few stones as possible along the way.

blocks.caption: Reach the last index using the fewest possible jumps

blocks.text: The starting position is already the last index, so 0 jumps are needed at all.
It is worth asking exactly what information about earlier indices actually still matters once a later index is reached.

blocks.title: How Should We Think?
blocks.text:
Observation 1: The dynamic programming brute force correctly checks every earlier index that could reach the current one, but most of that history is irrelevant, only the single farthest point reachable so far ever changes what happens next.

Observation 2: Best Time to Buy and Sell Stock already showed that a single running value, swept forward in one pass, can replace checking every earlier index individually.

Observation 3: Reframing the walk as expanding one full jump "level" at a time makes this concrete: this is exactly breadth first search explored layer by layer, where the current boundary marks how far the current number of jumps has already secured.

Observation 4: Tracking the single farthest index reachable while scanning within the current boundary, and only incrementing the jump count once that boundary itself is reached, correctly reproduces the DP answer, confirmed by tracing nums equal to [2, 3, 1, 1, 4] through to the correct answer, 2.
Recognizing this as breadth first search by levels, where the current boundary marks the edge of the current level, is what replaces a full history of reachability with two running integers.
Use dynamic programming: for every index, its minimum jump count is 1 plus the smallest minimum jump count among every earlier index that can reach it directly.

items: Create a dp array where dp[i] holds the minimum number of jumps to reach index i, starting with dp[0] equal to 0.
For every index i, look at every earlier index j that can jump far enough to reach i.
Set dp[i] to 1 plus the smallest dp[j] among all such j.
Return dp at the last index.

blocks.text: Why the code is written this way

items: dp[0] is seeded at 0 since reaching the starting index needs no jumps at all.
Every index i checks every earlier index j individually to see if j's jump range covers i, then takes the best, smallest, dp[j] among all qualifying j.
This directly implements the definition of minimum jumps as a shortest path style recurrence, but re-examines the full history of earlier indices for every single position.

blocks.text: Every index correctly considers every earlier index that could reach it, so the minimum jump count is found accurately.

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n squared), checking every pair of indices.
Space: O(n), for the dp array.
Limitation: most of these pairwise checks are unnecessary. What actually matters at each point is only how far the current jump can reach, not the full history of every index that could reach here.

blocks.title: The Optimization Journey
blocks.text:
Why the brute force works but is wasteful: it stores and reconsiders a full minimum jump count for every earlier index, even though only the single farthest reachable point among them ever influences what comes next.

What tracking a single running farthest point fixes directly: while scanning forward, keeping just the largest i plus nums[i] seen so far captures everything relevant about every index visited within the current jump.

What triggers a new jump: once the scan reaches the current boundary, meaning every index within the current jump's reach has been considered, a new jump must be taken, and the boundary extends to the farthest point found during that stretch.

The core idea: treat each jump as one full breadth first search level, expanding the boundary outward one level at a time instead of tracking a full per-index jump count.

Think of the walk as expanding one jump at a time, like exploring level by level. Track the farthest index reachable using the jumps taken so far (the current boundary), and separately track the farthest index reachable from anywhere within the current level while scanning forward. The moment the scan reaches the current boundary, a new jump must be taken, so the jump count increases and the boundary extends to the farthest reachable point found during that level.
Walk through the array once, tracking the current jump's boundary and the farthest reachable point seen so far.

blocks.caption: Optimized: expand level by level, jumping only when the current boundary is reached

codes.python:
def jump(nums):
    n = len(nums)
    jumps = 0
    current_boundary = 0
    farthest = 0
    for i in range(n - 1):
        farthest = max(farthest, i + nums[i])                    # farthest reachable from within this level
        if i == current_boundary:
            jumps += 1                                              # this level is exhausted, take a jump
            current_boundary = farthest
    return jumps


if __name__ == "__main__":
    nums = [2, 3, 1, 1, 4]
    print(jump(nums))

blocks.text: This works because the current boundary always marks the farthest point reachable using the jumps counted so far, so reaching that boundary while scanning means every option within the current jump has been considered, and the farthest point found during that scan is exactly the best possible reach for the next jump.

blocks.content: {"headers":["Case","What Happens","Result"],"rows":[["The scan index has not yet reached the current boundary","The farthest reachable value keeps updating without incrementing the jump count","Every option within the current jump is considered before committing to a new one"],["The scan index reaches the current boundary exactly","The jump count increases and the boundary is extended to the farthest value found","A new jump begins exactly when the previous one is fully exhausted"]]}

blocks.title: Time and Space Complexity
blocks.text:
Time: O(n), a single pass with constant work per index.
Space: O(1), only a few running values are kept.

blocks.text: This is the "implicit BFS by levels" pattern applied to an array instead of a graph: the current boundary marks the edge of the current BFS level, and crossing it always means a new level (a new jump) has begun.

items: Incrementing the jump count for every step instead of only when the current boundary is actually reached.
Forgetting to stop the loop one index early (at n minus 2, not n minus 1), since a jump taken exactly from the last index should never be counted.

blocks.text: Explicitly connect this greedy boundary expansion approach to breadth first search, describing each jump as fully exploring one BFS level before moving to the next, since interviewers often want to hear that connection made out loud.

blocks.title: If The Interviewer Says This, Think This
blocks.text:
If the interviewer says "can you avoid the full dp array", think: greedy level by level expansion, tracking only the current boundary and the farthest reach seen.
If the interviewer says "how is this related to BFS", think: each jump corresponds exactly to fully exploring one BFS level before advancing to the next.
If the interviewer says "what if you also needed the actual sequence of jumps", think: record the index where each new boundary was set, then reconstruct the path backward from those markers.

blocks.title: Complexity Summary
blocks.text: Brute force: O(n squared) time, O(n) space. Optimized: O(n) time, O(1) space.

items: Pattern: greedy level by level boundary expansion, the array equivalent of breadth first search layer by layer.

Core Idea: only the farthest reachable point matters at any moment, so tracking a current boundary and the farthest reach seen while scanning within it reproduces the true minimum jump count without a full dynamic programming table.
Time: O(n squared) for the brute force, O(n) for the optimized approach.
Space: O(n) for the brute force's dp array, O(1) for the optimized approach.
Most Important Observation: this is breadth first search in disguise, each jump is exactly one fully explored BFS level.
Interview Difficulty: the dynamic programming formulation is intuitive; recognizing and articulating the BFS-by-levels greedy reduction is what shows real depth.
One line memory trick: track the current boundary and the farthest reach, jump only when the boundary is reached.
